strengths: The paper investigates an important problem: maintaining selective attention when test contexts greatly exceed training lengths. Combining entmax with content-dependent temperature scaling and hybrid positional encodings is a plausible, practically simple approach.

The strongest synthetic results are impressive. ASEntmax with NAPE achieves 76.7% exact match on associative recall at 1024× training length, compared with 6.0% for adaptively scaled softmax, and 96.4% on Reverse at 4× length, compared with 28.5% for fixed-temperature entmax.

The evaluation covers several complementary synthetic tasks and includes useful appendix comparisons across positional encodings, adaptive softmax, and non-content-dependent scaling. The two-level-logit analysis also clearly illustrates when entmax can ignore arbitrarily many distractors.
weaknesses: The over-squashing guarantee is not established. Appendix C.3 derives an upper bound on gradient magnitude; reducing the number of terms does not imply larger gradients or a lower bound on retained information. Sparse attention can entirely disconnect a relevant token. Equations (60)–(61) also reverse the support relation: forward influence requires i to belong to the receiving token's support, rather than the receiving token belonging to i's support. Layer-averaged gradient norms do not resolve these issues.

The representation-preservation proof does not establish the stated result for an L-layer transformer. Appendix C.2 constructs a one-layer attention example but does not propagate its separation through the normalization, residual, and feed-forward operations of the specified architecture. Definition 2 concerns collapse among positions within one sequence, whereas the proposition compares final positions across two different sequences. These are different properties.

The positional-encoding theory contains false claims. Proposition 6(b) asserts that deleting paths at one layer prevents eventual concentration on token 1, although subsequent layers can restore those paths. For example, an identity attention matrix at one layer followed by matrices attending entirely to token 1 contradicts the assertion. Persistent positive connections also do not imply the claimed uniform geometric convergence without a lower bound on their weights.

The non-dispersion conclusions substantially exceed the guarantees. The entropy bound H(p) ≤ log|S| applies to any supported distribution and assumes sublinear support growth rather than proving it for learned entmax attention. Equal logits yield uniform attention even with entmax. The bounded-logit, fixed-temperature softmax result also does not directly cover the adaptive-temperature and positional-bias baselines used experimentally.

The model-selection protocol weakens the length-generalization evidence. Appendix G.2 selects checkpoints using performance at 8× training length, or 2×/4× for some configurations, and reports the best run across three seeds and multiple learning rates. Thus longer contexts influence selection, and neither typical performance nor variability is established. Explicit validation/test separation, matched search budgets, and results across all seeds are needed.

The broader practical significance remains unverified. The 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment fits learned position scalers but reports no comparative language-modeling quality or long-context downstream results; its aggregate scaling-fit R² is only 0.17. Synthetic gains are also task-dependent: SSMax outperforms ASEntmax on Copy, and all methods fail on Sort at 8× length. Runtime and memory measurements are absent. The empirical promise does not compensate for the unresolved soundness problems in the paper's central theoretical claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether exact attention sparsity improves length generalization. The distinction between softmax probability dilution and entmax invariance to sufficiently low-scoring distractors is useful.

Reported gains are substantial on selected synthetic tasks. With NAPE, ASEntmax achieves 76.7% exact match on MQMTAR at 65K tokens and 96.4% on Reverse at 4× training length. Appendix comparisons against adaptively scaled softmax and non-content-adaptive entmax strengthen these findings.
The experiments cover several complementary tasks and positional encodings, with substantial architectural and data-generation details in the appendices.
weaknesses: The over-squashing claim is not established. Appendix C.3 derives an upper bound on gradient magnitude; reducing the number of terms does not imply stronger gradients or a positive lower bound. Sparsity can eliminate every path from a relevant input. Equations (60)–(61) also reverse the support indexing: forward influence requires i to belong to the receiving token's support, not the receiving token to belong to i's support.

The representational-preservation proof does not establish the stated transformer result. Appendix C.2 analyzes a single attention-weighted average, omitting the normalization and FFN operations in the model definition and providing no multilayer extension. Its explicit d=1 example is particularly problematic with LayerNorm, which removes scalar input variation. Moreover, Definition 2 concerns all token pairs within one sequence, whereas the proposition compares final tokens across two sequences.

The positional-encoding theory contains substantive errors. Proposition 6(b) claims that deleting paths at one layer prevents eventual concentration on the first token, although later layers can restore those connections. Its claimed geometric decay also lacks a uniform positive transition bound. The RoPE analysis thresholds individual frequency contributions even though entmax thresholds their sum, so it does not establish the stated frequency-specific attention behavior.

Non-dispersion is overstated. Proposition 1 assumes sublinear support growth rather than proving that learned attention satisfies it; equal logits yield a uniform entmax distribution. The entropy bound H(p) ≤ log|S| is generic, and invariance to below-threshold additions does not guarantee that actual distractors remain below threshold. These conditional and existential results do not justify the broad prevention claims in the introduction and conclusion.

The evaluation reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, without variability estimates. Checkpoints are selected using extrapolation performance, typically at 8× training length, with task-dependent alternatives. This makes the results conditional on OOD model selection; separate validation/test samples, matched search budgets, and mean-and-variance reporting are needed to assess robustness.

Evidence for the proposed scaling law is limited. Gaussian range growth does not directly establish the temperature schedule needed to control entmax support. The motivating cancellation uses δ=0, while the experiments use δ=1. Appendix F.1 reports only R²=0.17 for the proposed fit, and comparisons against simpler fits do not isolate the benefit of the exponent from the added intercept and flexibility.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the conclusions suggest. The FineWeb experiment analyzes fitted scaling parameters rather than language-model quality or long-context performance. Synthetic results are also mixed: SSMax outperforms ASEntmax on Copy at 64×, all methods fail Sort at 8×, and several tasks are already solved by dense attention with suitable positional encoding. The promising retrieval and reversal results do not outweigh the unresolved theoretical and evaluation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether exact attention sparsity improves length extrapolation. Combining content-dependent temperature scaling with mixed NoPE/ALiBi heads is a practical and promising approach.

The strongest synthetic results are impressive: ASEntmax with NAPE achieves 76.7% exact match on associative recall at 1024× training length and 96.4% on reversal at 4× length, substantially outperforming the reported baselines.
The evaluation includes multiple tasks, positional encodings, and useful appendix comparisons against adaptive-scaled softmax and non-content-dependent entmax scaling.
The threshold-invariance and two-level-logit results provide useful intuition for how entmax can ignore additional distractors without diluting existing attention.
weaknesses: The over-squashing claim is not established. Appendix C.3 derives an upper bound on gradient magnitude; reducing its number of terms does not prove stronger gradients. Sparse attention can eliminate every path to a relevant token. Equations (60)–(61) also reverse the support membership needed for forward connectivity: the appropriate condition is i in S_k, rather than k in S_i.

The representational-preservation proof does not cover the stated transformer architecture. Appendix C.2 analyzes a single attention average, omitting the normalization and feed-forward transformations needed to establish the multilayer claim. Its explicit d=1 construction is incompatible with standard LayerNorm preserving the demonstrated differences. Moreover, Definition 2 concerns differences between arbitrary tokens, whereas the proposition concerns final tokens in two different sequences.

Additional theoretical statements are incorrect as written. Proposition 6 claims that deleting paths from token 1 at any single layer prevents eventual convergence to that token; subsequent layers can restore connectivity and convergence. Its geometric-decay argument also lacks a uniform positive bound on surviving attention weights.

The non-dispersion conclusions overstate the guarantees. The entropy bound H(p) ≤ log|S| is conditional on sublinear support, which is assumed rather than established for learned attention. Equal logits yield uniform entmax distributions at every length. These results demonstrate possible concentration, not general prevention of dispersion.

The evaluation reports only the best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, without variability. Checkpoints are selected using extrapolation performance, typically at 8× training length, with task-dependent alternatives. This is a legitimate development strategy if clearly separated from testing, but it weakens the interpretation of the reported results as unseen-length generalization; validation/test separation and selection budgets need clarification.

Evidence for practical long-context modeling remains limited to small synthetic-task transformers. The 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment fits learned positional scales but reports no comparative language-model quality or length-extrapolation results. Its overall proposed-fit R² of 0.17 also provides weak support for the scaling law. Runtime and memory measurements are absent.

The gains are not uniform: scalable softmax outperforms ASEntmax on long Copy sequences, and every method fails on Sort at 8× length. The promising empirical contribution does not compensate for the unresolved theoretical errors and experimental uncertainty at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important problem with a simple, implementable mechanism: content- and length-dependent scaling of entmax attention, compatible with existing AdaSplash kernels.

Reports substantial improvements under matched NAPE positional encodings: 95.3% associative-recall accuracy at 1024× training length, versus 26.7% for SSMax, and 97.4% retrieval accuracy at 16K after 2K-context language-model training.

Evaluation covers several synthetic tasks, language modeling, retrieval, and positional-encoding alternatives. Appendix comparisons with adaptively scaled softmax, top-k, and stick-breaking attention strengthen the synthetic evidence.
The threshold analysis usefully explains how entmax can preserve attention when additional logits fall below its support threshold.
weaknesses: The representational-preservation proof does not establish Proposition 2 as stated. Appendix D.2 explicitly constructs an original attention distribution with full support n, violating the proposition’s bounded-support assumption s ≪ n. It establishes a single attention-aggregation example without proving preservation through the stated depth-L architecture with normalization and feed-forward blocks.

The over-squashing argument does not prove stronger gradient signals. An upper bound on path count provides no lower bound on sensitivity; sparse attention can disconnect the relevant input entirely. Moreover, Equations 89–90 reverse the support indexing: forward propagation requires i to belong to the receiving token’s support, not the receiving token to belong to i’s support. Under causal masking, the written sets collapse to self-connections.

Appendix E.1 contains an additional false claim: deleting paths to token 1 at one layer does not prevent subsequent layers from restoring connectivity or convergence to token 1. The asserted geometric decay also lacks a uniform positive transition bound. These are substantive gaps in the theoretical contribution.

The non-dispersion conclusions exceed the guarantees. H(p) ≤ log |S| is a general entropy inequality, and sublinear support growth is assumed rather than established for trained models. Equal logits still produce uniform entmax attention. The fixed-temperature, bounded-logit softmax result also does not directly characterize the length-scaled or ALiBi baselines.

Synthetic results use the best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, with checkpoints selected using performance at up to 8× training length (Appendix G.2). This is disclosed, but means extrapolation informs model selection. Missing seed distributions, search budgets, and clearly separated validation/test protocols weaken confidence in the reported comparisons.

The most informative softmax control—ASSMax, using the proposed adaptive scaling—is evaluated on synthetic tasks but omitted from language modeling. Consequently, the language-model gains do not isolate sparsity from the more expressive temperature parameterization. Real-world evidence is also limited to one 420M model scale, two perplexity subsets, and two retrieval variants, without training-run uncertainty.

Benefits depend strongly on positional encoding and task. With RoPE+ABF, fixed entmax outperforms ASEntmax on both retrieval variants, including 32.4% versus 7.2% on S-NIAH-2 at 8K. SSMax wins on Copy, and all methods fail at 8× Sort. These results warrant narrower claims than consistent superiority. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: maintaining selective attention when inference contexts exceed training lengths. ASEntmax is a simple, implementable extension of entmax that is compatible with existing optimized kernels.

The reported empirical gains are substantial in several settings. ASEntmax achieves 95.3% MQMTAR accuracy at 1024× training length, versus 26.7% for SSMax, and 97.4% S-NIAH-1 retrieval accuracy at 16K tokens, versus 75.2%. The language-model perplexity improvements over SSMax provide evidence beyond synthetic tasks.

The appendices include extensive positional-encoding comparisons, synthetic-task baselines, and training details. The two-level-logit analysis usefully illustrates how entmax can preserve attention mass when added distractors fall below its threshold.
weaknesses: The over-squashing claim is not established by its proof. Appendix D.3 derives an upper bound on gradient magnitude and counts surviving paths; neither establishes stronger gradients than softmax. Sparse attention can eliminate every path from a relevant distant token. Moreover, Equations 89–90 reverse the support relation: a forward path requires the previous token to belong to the next token's attention support. As written, the causal constraints make these sets contain only the current token. This undermines a central theoretical contribution.

The representation-preservation proof does not establish Proposition 2 under its stated assumptions. Appendix D.2 explicitly constructs an original attention distribution with support n, violating the proposition's bounded-support assumption. Its derivation analyzes a single attention aggregation without establishing preservation through the stated L-layer transformer with normalization and feed-forward blocks. The scalar example also cannot directly validate the specified LayerNorm architecture.

Proposition 5 contains incorrect claims about products of dynamic attention matrices. Deleting paths to token 1 at one layer does not prevent subsequent layers from restoring its influence. For example, an identity attention matrix followed repeatedly by a causal matrix whose second row is [1/2, 1/2] eventually concentrates the second token's cumulative attention on token 1. Persistent connectivity alone also does not imply the asserted uniform geometric decay without additional quantitative assumptions.

The non-dispersion conclusions are substantially broader than the results. The entropy bound H(p) ≤ log |S| holds for any supported distribution, and sublinear support growth is assumed rather than established for learned entmax attention. Equal logits produce uniform attention even with entmax. The softmax result requires uniformly bounded logits and fixed temperature, so it does not establish an inherent disadvantage against the length-dependent scaling baselines or unbounded ALiBi biases used experimentally.

Experimental selection limits confidence in robustness. Appendix G.2 reports the best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, with checkpoints selected using extrapolation lengths, rather than means and variability. This does not invalidate extrapolation beyond those validation lengths, but it makes the headline results evidence of selected-model performance rather than reliable training outcomes. Validation/test separation and tuning budgets need clearer reporting.

The language-model experiments omit the matched adaptive-scaling softmax baseline, ASSMax, although it appears in several synthetic experiments. Consequently, the practical gains do not fully isolate sparsity from the more expressive scaling parameterization. Evaluation is also limited to one 420M model configuration and two simple retrieval variants; broader long-context understanding and computational overhead are not assessed.

Claims of consistent superiority overlook important counterevidence. SSMax outperforms ASEntmax on Copy, and Table 17 shows RoPE+ABF entmax outperforming ASEntmax on both retrieval variants at their longest reported lengths. These dependencies on task and positional encoding should qualify the conclusions. Overall, the promising empirical results do not outweigh the unresolved mathematical errors and evaluation limitations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: maintaining useful attention patterns when inference contexts substantially exceed training lengths. Combining entmax with content-dependent, per-head scaling is practical and compatible with existing optimized kernels.

The strongest empirical results are compelling: ASEntmax reaches 95.3% MQMTAR accuracy at 1024× training length and 97.4% S-NIAH-1 accuracy at 16K tokens, compared with 75.2% for SSMax. Long-context perplexity also improves over SSMax on both ArXiv and PubMed.

The experimental coverage includes multiple synthetic tasks, 420M-parameter language models, several positional encodings, and useful supplementary comparisons with adaptive-scaled softmax, top-k, and stick-breaking attention. The invariance to adding below-threshold logits provides a valid conceptual motivation.
weaknesses: The over-squashing result is not established by its proof. Appendix D.3 derives an upper bound on gradient norms and counts surviving paths; neither implies stronger gradients or greater sensitivity to distant inputs. Sparsity can disconnect the relevant input entirely. Moreover, Equations 89–90 reverse the support relationship: forward influence requires the source to belong to the destination's attention support. Under causal masking, the written sets contain only the current token. This undermines a central theoretical contribution.

The representational-preservation proof does not establish Proposition 2 as stated. The construction in Appendix D.2 explicitly gives the original sequence dense attention with support n, violating the proposition's assumption of support at most s much smaller than n. It analyzes a single attention aggregation without proving preservation through the stated L-layer architecture with normalization and feed-forward blocks.

Additional theoretical claims require correction. Proposition 1's concentration bound assumes sublinear support rather than showing that entmax learns or maintains it; equal logits still produce uniform attention for every alpha. Proposition 5 also incorrectly concludes that deleting paths at one layer prevents eventual convergence to the first token: subsequent layers can restore mixing. Its geometric convergence claim requires stronger conditions than persistent connectivity. The paper therefore overstates what its theory guarantees.

Synthetic evaluation reports the single best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates, with checkpoint selection based on performance at up to 8× training length (Appendix G.2). This measures extrapolation after longer-context model selection, and provides no estimate of typical performance or variability. Separate validation/test samples, matched search budgets, and aggregate results across seeds are needed to establish robustness.

The crucial matched adaptive-scaled softmax baseline appears in some synthetic experiments but is absent from language modeling. Consequently, the language-model results do not isolate the benefit of sparse attention from the more expressive scaling parameterization. The proposed method combines established entmax and adaptive-temperature ideas, making this attribution particularly important.

The broader claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Language modeling uses one model size and two simple RULER variants, without reported uncertainty or throughput/memory measurements. Gains depend strongly on positional encoding: with RoPE plus ABF, fixed entmax outperforms ASEntmax on both reported retrieval variants at their longest lengths. SSMax also wins on Copy. These limitations do not erase the promising empirical results, but together with the unresolved proof errors leave the submission below the acceptance threshold.
